items.stem: Which of the following best describes "globalisation"?
options: The increasing interconnection of the world's economies, cultures and peoples through trade, investment, technology, migration and communication
The international organisation, founded in 1995, that sets and enforces rules for trade between its members
The use of standard shipping containers from the 1950s, which greatly reduced the cost of transporting goods
Contracting another company, often abroad, to carry out work previously done in-house
items.answer: The increasing interconnection of the world's economies, cultures and peoples through trade, investment, technology, migration and communication
items.markingKey: A. "globalisation" is the increasing interconnection of the world's economies, cultures and peoples through trade, investment, technology, migration and communication.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Bandung Conference"?
options: The process by which colonies gained independence from colonial powers, mainly between 1945 and 1975
The South African body (1996–2003) that heard testimony on apartheid-era human rights violations
The killing of 69 people by South African police at an anti-pass-law protest on 21 March 1960
The 1955 meeting in Indonesia of 29 Asian and African states opposing colonialism
items.answer: The 1955 meeting in Indonesia of 29 Asian and African states opposing colonialism
items.markingKey: D. "Bandung Conference" is the 1955 meeting in Indonesia of 29 Asian and African states opposing colonialism.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Einsatzgruppen"?
options: A moment after which the course of events changes decisively
Acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group (UN Genocide Convention, 1948)
Hostility to, prejudice against or discrimination against Jews
Mobile killing units that murdered Jews and others in mass shootings in the occupied Soviet territories from 1941
items.answer: Mobile killing units that murdered Jews and others in mass shootings in the occupied Soviet territories from 1941
items.markingKey: D. "Einsatzgruppen" is mobile killing units that murdered Jews and others in mass shootings in the occupied Soviet territories from 1941.

items.stem: Distinguish between population density and population distribution.
items.answer: Distribution describes where people live; density measures how many people live per unit area.
items.markingKey: Distribution describes where people live; density measures how many people live per unit area. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Communist states in practice achieved a classless, stateless society." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Soviet communism created a powerful state and a new privileged party elite, far from Marx's ideal.
items.markingKey: Soviet communism created a powerful state and a new privileged party elite, far from Marx's ideal. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between the revolutions of 1989 in Poland and Hungary and the revolution in Romania.
items.answer: Poland and Hungary saw negotiated, peaceful transitions; Romania's revolution was violent and ended with the execution of Ceaușescu.
items.markingKey: Poland and Hungary saw negotiated, peaceful transitions; Romania's revolution was violent and ended with the execution of Ceaușescu. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Source A – Historian's interpretation (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Fritz Fischer, Griff nach der Weltmacht (Germany's Aims in the First World War), Düsseldorf, 1961

The historian argued that Germany's leaders deliberately pursued aggressive aims before 1914, seeking to dominate Europe and expand overseas, and that they used the July Crisis to launch a war they had long considered.

Identify two points that Source A makes about the long-term causes of the First World War: militarism, alliances, imperialism and nationalism, using evidence from the source.
items.answer: Germany bore primary responsibility because of its aggressive war aims.
items.markingKey: Germany bore primary responsibility because of its aggressive war aims. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [5]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem:
Source A – Academic study (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Erica Chenoweth and Maria J. Stephan, Why Civil Resistance Works, New York, 2011

The researchers found that between 1900 and 2006 non-violent resistance campaigns were about twice as likely to succeed as violent campaigns, partly because they attracted wider participation and caused defections among security forces.

Identify two points that Source A makes about active citizenship: protest, the media and digital participation, using evidence from the source.
items.answer: Non-violent resistance is more effective than violent resistance.
items.markingKey: Non-violent resistance is more effective than violent resistance. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [5]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem:
Source A – Assessment guidance (paraphrased): Paraphrase of typical IB MYP Individuals and Societies eAssessment markband descriptors for extended response tasks

The guidance stated that the highest-scoring responses present a sustained, well-supported argument that consistently addresses the question, use relevant and accurate evidence, consider different perspectives and reach a well-reasoned conclusion.

Explain one value and one limitation of Source A for an investigation into extended response writing: argument, evidence, counter-argument and conclusion (Criteria C and D), referring to its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of typical IB MYP Individuals and Societies eAssessment markband descriptors for extended response tasks. Purpose: to explain to teachers and students how extended responses are assessed. Value: It shows directly what examiners reward. Limitation: It describes standards in general terms; applying them requires examples.

items.stem: Evaluate the research question "Is globalisation good or bad?" for an MYP Individuals and Societies investigation into the winners and losers of globalisation: jobs, culture and inequality. Rewrite it so that it is clear, focused and researchable.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a vague value question Improved: "How far has Vietnam's integration into global supply chains since 1986 reduced poverty?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a vague value question); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How far has Vietnam's integration into global supply chains since 1986 reduced poverty?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Describe the research methods you would use to answer "How has the length of the growing season in Punjab changed since 1970, and is this consistent with climate change?", naming specific sources and explaining why each is appropriate.
items.answer: Use IMD temperature data, crop calendars and two studies; graph trends; evaluate data; cite in APA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Use IMD temperature data, crop calendars and two studies; graph trends; evaluate data; cite in APA. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Felix argues that "Non-violent protest was the most important factor in the success of the civil rights movement." Mei disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Non-violent protest was central to the legislative breakthroughs, but it worked with legal challenges, federal action and the wider political context.
items.markingKey: Felix: campaigns like Birmingham and Selma led directly to the 1964 and 1965 Acts. Mei: NAACP legal victories such as Brown v. Board were crucial. Judgement (1-2 marks): Non-violent protest was central to the legislative breakthroughs, but it worked with legal challenges, federal action and the wider political context.

items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why Stalin introduced the Five-Year Plans.
items.answer: He wanted to industrialise rapidly to catch up with the West, build military strength against perceived threats, and create a socialist economy and working class.
items.markingKey: Content: He wanted to industrialise rapidly to catch up with the West, build military strength against perceived threats, and create a socialist economy and working class. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "China's one-child policy was a success." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: It achieved its numerical aim, but at high human and demographic cost, and similar declines were achieved elsewhere without coercion, so "success" is highly questionable.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it may have prevented hundreds of millions of births and eased pressure on resources; it supported rapid economic growth. Counter-arguments: fertility was already falling; development explains much of the decline; it caused human rights abuses, a gender imbalance and rapid ageing. Thesis/conclusion: It achieved its numerical aim, but at high human and demographic cost, and similar declines were achieved elsewhere without coercion, so "success" is highly questionable. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The Universal Declaration of Human Rights has been effective in protecting human rights."
items.answer: The UDHR has been highly influential in shaping law and norms, but its effectiveness depends on enforcement, which remains uneven.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it set a global standard and inspired constitutions and treaties; it underpins courts, NGOs and campaigns worldwide. Arguments against: it is not binding and is widely violated; enforcement depends on states and is weakened by power politics. Supported judgement: The UDHR has been highly influential in shaping law and norms, but its effectiveness depends on enforcement, which remains uneven. Markbands (8 marks): MYP I&S criterion D (year 5), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly discusses concepts, issues, models and theories, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, effectively analyses and evaluates a wide range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and thoroughly interprets a range of perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The ability to access, analyse and evaluate media critically"?
items.answer: media literacy
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of media literacy.

items.stem: What should a researcher obtain before interviewing people?
items.answer: Informed consent
items.markingKey: A. Participants must know how their information will be used.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The June 1947 plan for partition and the transfer of power, brought forward to August 1947"?
items.answer: Mountbatten Plan
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of Mountbatten Plan.

items.stem: Explain the difference between Ghana's path to independence and Kenya's path to independence.
items.answer: Ghana gained independence peacefully through mass politics and elections; Kenya's involved the violent Mau Mau rebellion and harsh British repression.
items.markingKey: Ghana gained independence peacefully through mass politics and elections; Kenya's involved the violent Mau Mau rebellion and harsh British repression. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "The USA defeated the USSR militarily to end the Cold War." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The Cold War ended without direct war, mainly through Soviet internal crisis, reform and popular movements in Eastern Europe.
items.markingKey: The Cold War ended without direct war, mainly through Soviet internal crisis, reform and popular movements in Eastern Europe. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why collectivisation caused famine.
items.answer: Peasants resisted by slaughtering livestock, experienced farmers were deported, production fell, and the state still requisitioned grain, leaving rural areas without food. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Peasants resisted by slaughtering livestock, experienced farmers were deported, production fell, and the state still requisitioned grain, leaving rural areas without food. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

The prime minister of a Caribbean island state told world leaders that a 2 °C rise would be a death sentence for small island states, and called for reform of global finance to help vulnerable countries adapt and recover from climate disasters.

Explain one value and one limitation of Source A for an investigation into the impacts of climate change on people and places, referring to its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of Mia Mottley, Prime Minister of Barbados, speech at COP26, Glasgow, 1 November 2021. Purpose: to urge leaders to act on climate change and climate finance. items.stem:
Source A – Report (paraphrased): Paraphrase of International Commission on Intervention and State Sovereignty, The Responsibility to Protect, Ottawa, 2001

The commission argued that state sovereignty implies responsibility, and that when a population is suffering serious harm and the state is unwilling or unable to stop it, the principle of non-intervention yields to the international responsibility to protect.

Explain one value and one limitation of Source A for an investigation into political systems and sovereignty: democracy, authoritarianism and the role of the United Nations, referring to its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of International Commission on Intervention and State Sovereignty, The Responsibility to Protect, Ottawa, 2001. Purpose: to reconcile sovereignty with humanitarian intervention after Rwanda and Kosovo. Value: It shaped the principle later endorsed by the UN. Limitation: It sets out principles but critics fear powerful states may use it for their own ends.

items.stem:
Source A – Charter (paraphrased): Paraphrase of the Preamble to the Charter of the United Nations, San Francisco, 26 June 1945

The founding document states that the peoples of the United Nations are determined to save future generations from the scourge of war, which twice in their lifetime had brought untold sorrow, and to reaffirm faith in fundamental human rights and the equal rights of nations large and small.

How reliable is Source A for someone researching the consequences of the war: the United Nations and a new world order? Justify your answer using its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of the Preamble to the Charter of the United Nations, San Francisco, 26 June 1945. Purpose: to set out the purposes of the new organisation and win support for it. Value: It shows the aims and values agreed by the founding states. Limitation: It states ideals; it does not show how far states lived up to them, and it was shaped by the victorious powers.

items.stem: Describe the research methods you would use to answer "How did the experiences of Indian soldiers on the Western Front in 1914–15 compare with those of British soldiers?", naming specific sources and explaining why each is appropriate.
items.answer: Use censored letters, war diaries and two historians; compare conditions; evaluate sources; cite in MLA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Use censored letters, war diaries and two historians; compare conditions; evaluate sources; cite in MLA. items.stem: You have three weeks to investigate "How significant was the secret agreement on the Turkish missiles in resolving the Cuban Missile Crisis?" Outline a step-by-step plan, the sources you would use and one way you would evaluate your process at the end.
items.answer: Use the ExComm tapes, Khrushchev's letters and two historians; compare public and secret accounts; evaluate sources; cite in MLA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Use the ExComm tapes, Khrushchev's letters and two historians; compare public and secret accounts; evaluate sources; cite in MLA. items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why global governance is needed.
items.answer: Problems such as climate change, pandemics, trade and conflict cross borders and cannot be solved by one state alone.
items.markingKey: Content: Problems such as climate change, pandemics, trade and conflict cross borders and cannot be solved by one state alone. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. items.stem: Using accurate subject terminology and at least one specific example, write a structured paragraph that responds to: Explain why population density varies within countries.
items.answer: Physical factors such as relief, climate, water and soil, and human factors such as jobs, transport and services, make some areas attractive and others hostile.
items.markingKey: Content: Physical factors such as relief, climate, water and soil, and human factors such as jobs, transport and services, make some areas attractive and others hostile. items.stem: "Natural factors explain most of the climate change observed since 1950." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Natural factors cause variation, but the evidence overwhelmingly shows that recent warming is driven by human greenhouse gas emissions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: climate has changed naturally in the past, e.g. ice ages; volcanoes and solar cycles affect temperature. Arguments against: solar output has not increased since 1950 while temperatures have risen; the IPCC concludes it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the climate. Supported judgement: Natural factors cause variation, but the evidence overwhelmingly shows that recent warming is driven by human greenhouse gas emissions. Markbands (8 marks): MYP I&S criterion D (year 5), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly discusses concepts, issues, models and theories, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, effectively analyses and evaluates a wide range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and thoroughly interprets a range of perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem:
Source A – Historian's interpretation (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Ian Kershaw, The "Hitler Myth": Image and Reality in the Third Reich, Oxford, 1987

The historian argued that Hitler's power rested heavily on a "Hitler myth" – an image of a leader above party politics who embodied the nation – created by propaganda and sustained by foreign policy successes, and that it declined as the war turned against Germany.

"Propaganda was more important than terror in maintaining Nazi control of Germany." Using Source A and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree?
items.answer: Historians such as Ian Kershaw argue that consent and coercion worked together: propaganda won many, while terror targeted those who would not conform.
items.markingKey: From the source: Propaganda created an image of Hitler that underpinned the regime's popularity. Own knowledge for: propaganda created the Hitler myth and genuine popularity among many; economic recovery and full employment, publicised by propaganda, won support. Own knowledge against: the Gestapo, camps and informers crushed opposition; fear of denunciation silenced critics. Judgement: Historians such as Ian Kershaw argue that consent and coercion worked together: propaganda won many, while terror targeted those who would not conform. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. MYP I&S criterion D (year 5), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly discusses concepts, issues, models and theories, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, effectively analyses and evaluates a wide range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and thoroughly interprets a range of perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "sea-level rise"?
options: Actions that reduce vulnerability to climate impacts, such as flood defences, drought-resistant crops and early warning systems
The increase in average sea level caused by thermal expansion of water and melting ice
An economic system that keeps materials in use through reuse, repair, remanufacturing and recycling, designing out waste
The combination of sources used to generate a country's energy, such as coal, gas, nuclear, hydro, wind and solar
items.answer: The increase in average sea level caused by thermal expansion of water and melting ice
items.markingKey: B. "sea-level rise" is the increase in average sea level caused by thermal expansion of water and melting ice.

items.stem: On what date did the Berlin Wall open?
items.answer: 9 November 1989
items.markingKey: A. Crowds crossed after a confused announcement.

items.stem: Which country, south of the equator, was placed in the "North" on the Brandt line?
items.answer: Australia (and New Zealand)
items.markingKey: D. The line curves around them.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the UDHR was adopted in 1948.
items.answer: After the Holocaust and the war, states wanted a common standard of rights to prevent such atrocities and to show that how a state treats its people is a matter of international concern. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the Montreal Protocol succeeded where climate agreements have struggled.
items.answer: CFC substitutes were available and affordable, a small number of industries were involved, the science was clear, and a fund helped developing countries comply. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: CFC substitutes were available and affordable, a small number of industries were involved, the science was clear, and a fund helped developing countries comply. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Adaptation means giving up on stopping climate change." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Adaptation complements mitigation; both are needed.
items.markingKey: Adaptation complements mitigation; both are needed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source A – Political writing (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, The Communist Manifesto, London, 1848

The authors argued that the history of all existing society is the history of class struggles, and that the working class would overthrow capitalism and create a society without classes, in which the means of production would be owned in common.

According to Source A, what can we learn about political ideologies: democracy, communism, fascism and Nazism? Support your answer with details from the source.
items.answer: Class struggle drives history and workers will create a classless society.
items.markingKey: Class struggle drives history and workers will create a classless society. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [5]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: Noah argues that "Stalin's economic policies were a success." Alessia disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: In industrial and military terms they achieved much, but at an enormous human cost; whether this counts as success depends on the criteria used.

items.answer: It achieved its numerical aim, but at high human and demographic cost, and similar declines were achieved elsewhere without coercion, so "success" is highly questionable.

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "International pressure was the main reason apartheid ended." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.

items.answer: Stalingrad was arguably the decisive turning point in Europe, but the war was global; Midway and US entry were equally important in the Pacific.

An Indian soldier wounded in France wrote home that the fighting was unlike anything known before, with constant shelling and many comrades killed. He asked his family not to worry and said he was proud to have done his duty, but described the cold and the losses.

How reliable is Source A for someone researching the experience of war: trench warfare, the home front and colonial soldiers, including Indian troops? Justify your answer using its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Composite paraphrase of letters by Indian soldiers, 1915, from the censored mail extracts collected by the Indian Mail Censor (published in David Omissi, Indian Voices of the Great War, 1999). Purpose: to communicate personal experiences to family in India. Value: It is a rare first-hand account from a colonial soldier. Limitation: Letters were censored, so soldiers may have avoided criticism; they were also often written by scribes.

items.stem:
Source A – Charter (paraphrased): Paraphrase of the Preamble to the Charter of the United Nations, San Francisco, 26 June 1945

The founding document states that the peoples of the United Nations are determined to save future generations from the scourge of war, which twice in their lifetime had brought untold sorrow, and to reaffirm faith in fundamental human rights and the equal rights of nations large and small.

Explain one value and one limitation of Source A for an investigation into the consequences of the war: the United Nations and a new world order, referring to its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of the Preamble to the Charter of the United Nations, San Francisco, 26 June 1945. Purpose: to set out the purposes of the new organisation and win support for it. Value: It shows the aims and values agreed by the founding states. Limitation: It states ideals; it does not show how far states lived up to them, and it was shaped by the victorious powers.

items.stem: Zara is investigating the US civil rights movement: Martin Luther King, Malcolm X and non-violent protest and proposes the research question: "Who was Martin Luther King?" Explain one weakness of this research question and write a more focused alternative.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a biographical question Improved: "How far did television coverage of the Birmingham campaign influence the passing of the Civil Rights Act of 1964?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a biographical question); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How far did television coverage of the Birmingham campaign influence the passing of the Civil Rights Act of 1964?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Formulate an action plan to investigate the research question "How far did the reparations of the Treaty of Versailles cause the German hyperinflation of 1923?" Include the main steps, at least one primary and one secondary source, and how you would record your findings.
items.answer: Use exchange-rate data, reparation schedules and two historians; compare causes such as war debts and money printing; cite in MLA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Use exchange-rate data, reparation schedules and two historians; compare causes such as war debts and money printing; cite in MLA. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why globalisation can increase inequality within countries.
items.answer: Gains go to skilled workers, capital owners and connected regions, while unskilled workers and peripheral regions face competition and lose out.
items.markingKey: Content: Gains go to skilled workers, capital owners and connected regions, while unskilled workers and peripheral regions face competition and lose out. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why China introduced the one-child policy in 1980.
items.answer: Leaders feared that rapid population growth would prevent economic modernisation and strain food and resources, so they aimed to cap the population at about 1.2 billion by 2000.

items.stem:
Source A – Poster (described): Soviet propaganda poster celebrating Yuri Gagarin's flight, published by the state publisher, Moscow, 1961

A Soviet poster from 1961 shows a smiling cosmonaut in a helmet with the letters of the USSR, a rocket rising behind him, and a slogan celebrating the glory of the Soviet people who opened the way to space.

"The nuclear arms race made the world safer during the Cold War." Using Source A and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree?
items.answer: Deterrence may have prevented a direct superpower war, but the arms race created serious risks of catastrophe; "safer" is debatable.
items.markingKey: From the source: The Soviet people and system led humanity into space. Own knowledge for: MAD deterred direct war between the superpowers; crises such as Cuba led to arms control. Own knowledge against: the world came close to nuclear war in 1962 and 1983; enormous resources were diverted and tests harmed people and environments. Judgement: Deterrence may have prevented a direct superpower war, but the arms race created serious risks of catastrophe; "safer" is debatable. items.stem: "The WTO has been more successful than regional trade blocs in promoting free trade." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: The WTO built the base of global trade rules, but recent progress has come mostly from regional and bilateral agreements.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: WTO rules cover almost all world trade and have a dispute system; tariffs have fallen greatly since GATT in 1947. Arguments against: the Doha Round failed and the dispute appellate body has been paralysed since 2019; regional blocs such as the EU and RCEP have achieved deeper integration. Supported judgement: The WTO built the base of global trade rules, but recent progress has come mostly from regional and bilateral agreements.
